title: The vocal tract, constrictions and the vowels /i/, /a/ and /u/

blocks.main: **The air in the vocal tract is a fixed-free system that vibrates back and forth along the tube.** It is **fixed at the glottis**, because the closed vocal folds stop the air there from moving, so the air can only be compressed. It is **free at the lips**, where the air moves in and out.
sub: Where the air on both sides moves toward a spot, the air there is compressed. Where it moves away, the air there spreads out.
So the air is compressed the most where it moves the least, and it moves the most where it is compressed the least.
With no constriction, as in **done**, the vowel is **schwa**, and the formants are about **500, 1500 and 2500 Hz**.
blocks.end: That is why a constriction does different things in different places.

blocks.ref: Lecture 12 · p16 · Lecture 13 · p12 · Lecture 14 · p8
blocks.main: **Vowels differ in the shape of the vocal tract, which depends on where the tongue makes a constriction and whether the lips are rounded.** A **constriction** is a narrowing of the tube. With the tongue high and front, the result is the vowel in **dean**.
sub: With the tongue high and back and the lips rounded, the result is the vowel in **dune**.
With the tongue low, the result is an open vowel like the one in **Don**.
blocks.end: So the same voice from the vocal folds can make different vowels, because each constriction changes the formants.

blocks.main: **A constriction packs the air into a smaller space, so the air there becomes both heavier (denser) and stiffer.** What the constriction does to a formant depends on what the air at that spot is doing in that mode.
sub: To work out the effect, find the constriction and decide whether the air there is mostly **moving** or mostly **compressed** in that mode.
If the air is mostly moving, the extra mass counts, so the formant goes **down**.
If the air is mostly compressed, the extra stiffness counts, so the formant goes **up**.
blocks.end: So a large rise in a formant means the air there was springy and hardly moving, and a large fall means it was moving a lot.

blocks.ref: Lecture 12 · p19 · Lecture 13 · p16 · Lecture 14 · p11
blocks.main: **For /u/, as in dune, F1 and F2 both go down.** **Lip rounding** makes the constriction at the lips, which is the free end of the tube.
sub: In **Mode 1**, the air at the lips is moving, so the extra mass counts and **F1 goes down**.
In **Mode 2**, the air at the lips is also moving, so the extra mass counts and **F2 goes down**.
blocks.end: So at the lips only the extra mass matters, because the air there moves in every mode.

blocks.ref: Lecture 12 · p20 · Lecture 13 · p17, 21 · Lecture 14 · p12
blocks.main: **For /i/, as in dean, F1 goes down and F2 goes up.** The constriction is about **two-thirds of the way from the glottis**, near the front of the vocal tract.
sub: In **Mode 1**, the air at that spot is moving, so the extra mass counts and **F1 goes down**.
In **Mode 2**, the air at that spot is compressed, so the extra stiffness counts and **F2 goes up**.
blocks.end: So the formants of /i/ **move apart**, because one constriction sits on a moving spot in one mode and a springy spot in the other.

blocks.ref: Lecture 12 · p21 · Lecture 13 · p18, 22 · Lecture 14 · p13
blocks.main: **For /a/, as in Don, F1 goes up and F2 goes down.** The constriction is about **one-third of the way from the glottis**, toward the back of the throat.
sub: In **Mode 1**, the air at that spot is compressed, so the extra stiffness counts and **F1 goes up**.
In **Mode 2**, the air at that spot is moving, so the extra mass counts and **F2 goes down**.
blocks.end: So the formants of /a/ **move together**, the opposite of /i/.

questions.q: If I constrict the vocal tract somewhere and I raise the formant a great deal, what must be true of air motion versus springiness at this location?
questions.a: At that location the air must be very springy and hardly moving in that mode. A constriction adds both mass and stiffness, and the formant went up, so the added stiffness is what counted. Stiffness only counts where the air is compressed and expanded. The added mass did nothing, because the air there was not moving.

questions.q: If I constrict the vocal tract somewhere and I lower the formant a great deal, what must be true at this location?
questions.a: At that location the air must be moving a lot and hardly compressed in that mode. The formant went down, so the added mass is what counted, and mass only counts where the air is moving. This is what happens at the lips for /u/.

questions.q: A classmate says more mass lowers the frequency and more stiffness raises it, so a constriction always cancels out. What is wrong with this argument?
questions.a: The argument is wrong because, in any one mode, only one of the two changes matters at most locations. If the air at the constriction is mostly moving, it is not being compressed, so only the extra mass counts and the formant goes down. If the air there is mostly compressed, it is not moving, so only the extra stiffness counts and the formant goes up. That is why the same constriction can push F1 and F2 in opposite directions.

questions.q: Why is the air in the vocal tract a fixed-free system? Say which end is which.
questions.a: The glottis end is the fixed end, and the lip end is the free end. The glottis end is closed off by the vocal folds, so the air there cannot move and can only be compressed and expanded. The lip end is open, so the air there moves freely in and out without being compressed against anything.

questions.q: Compared with done, what happens to F1 and F2 in dune, and why?
questions.a: Both F1 and F2 go down in dune. Lip rounding creates a constriction at the free end, where the air moves the most in every mode. So the added mass counts in both Mode 1 and Mode 2, and extra mass at a moving location lowers the frequency.

questions.q: Compared with done, what happens to F1 and F2 in dean, and why?
questions.a: In dean, F1 goes down and F2 goes up. The constriction is about two-thirds of the way from the glottis. In Mode 1 the air there is moving, so the added mass lowers F1. In Mode 2 the air there is compressed, so the added stiffness raises F2.

questions.q: Compared with done, what happens to F1 and F2 in Don, and why?
questions.a: In Don, F1 goes up and F2 goes down. The constriction is about one-third of the way from the glottis. In Mode 1 the air there is compressed, so the added stiffness raises F1. In Mode 2 the air there is moving, so the added mass lowers F2.

questions.q: A new constriction is placed deep in the throat, one-fifth of the way from the glottis, where the air is compressed in both Mode 1 and Mode 2. What happens to F1 and F2?
questions.a: Both F1 and F2 go up. The location is near the fixed end, where the air is compressed in both modes. So the added stiffness is what counts in both modes, and extra stiffness raises the frequency.

questions.q: Why does rounding the lips lower every formant?
questions.a: Rounding the lips lowers every formant because the lips are the free end of the vocal tract. The free end is a location of maximum motion in every mode. So a constriction there adds mass where the air is moving, and that lowers every formant. Adding mass at the top of a building lowers every mode for the same reason.

title: Spectra, spectrograms and speech over time

blocks.main: **A spectrum shows a sound at one instant, and a spectrogram lines up many spectra over time.** In a spectrum, frequency is on the horizontal axis and amplitude is on the vertical axis. In a **spectrogram**, time is on the horizontal axis, frequency is on the vertical axis and **darkness** shows amplitude.
sub: The **dark bands are the formants**, because the harmonics near each formant are the loudest.
F1 is the lowest dark band, and F2 is the next one up.
blocks.end: So the bands rise and fall as the vocal tract changes shape.

blocks.main: **Each vowel moves the formant bands away from schwa in its own direction.** From schwa to /i/, the bands **move apart**. From schwa to /u/, **both bands drop**. From schwa to /a/, the bands **move together**.
sub: Going from /i/ to /a/, F1 rises and F2 falls.

blocks.main: **In connected speech the formants never stay still, because every sound moves the constriction.** In "Where were you a year ago?", F2 rises when the tongue moves toward /i/. The formants drop when the lips round for the /u/ of you.
sub: When the tongue moves back and down toward an /a/-like sound, F1 rises and F2 falls.
blocks.end: So speech is a continuous series of constrictions, not a list of separate vowels.

blocks.main: **Listeners identify a consonant partly from the vowel after it.** In **Malécot**'s work in the 1950s, the m of ma was joined to the a of na. Listeners heard na.
sub: The vowel from na still carried the formant transition left by the n, and listeners used that transition.
blocks.end: So listeners decide on the consonant during the vowel, after the consonant is over.

questions.q: Describe a spectrogram.
questions.a: A spectrogram lines up many spectra side by side over time. Time runs along the horizontal axis and frequency runs up the vertical axis. The darkness of each spot shows how much amplitude there is at that frequency and time. The formants appear as dark bands, so you can follow them as they rise and fall, for example F1 rising and F2 falling from /i/ to /a/.

questions.q: How is a spectrum different from a spectrogram?
questions.a: A spectrum shows one instant, and a spectrogram shows how the spectrum changes over time. A spectrum has frequency on the horizontal axis and amplitude on the vertical axis. A spectrogram has time on the horizontal axis and frequency on the vertical axis, with amplitude shown as darkness. Real speech is always changing, so a spectrogram shows the formants moving.

questions.q: A speaker starts on schwa and switches to another vowel. F1 goes down and F2 goes up. Which vowel? What if both go down?
questions.a: When F1 goes down and F2 goes up, the vowel is /i/ as in dean, and the two bands move apart. When both F1 and F2 go down, the vowel is /u/ as in dune, because lip rounding lowers every formant.

questions.q: Describe the spectrogram of a speaker going from schwa to the vowel of Don.
questions.a: F1 goes up and F2 goes down, so the two lowest dark bands move toward each other. The constriction for Don is one-third of the way from the glottis. The air there is compressed in Mode 1, so the added stiffness raises F1. The air there is moving in Mode 2, so the added mass lowers F2.

questions.q: Why do listeners hear na when the m of ma is joined to the a of na?
questions.a: Listeners hear na because the information about the consonant is carried mostly by the vowel that follows it. After n, one formant of the vowel drops, and after m, that formant stays flat. So the a from na still signals n. Listeners decide which consonant they heard during the vowel, after the consonant is over.

title: The sigmoid and where the idea came from

blocks.main: **The sigmoid is a function that takes a neuron's inner product and returns a number between 0 and 1.** A large negative input gives about **0**, which is off. A large positive input gives about **1**, which is on. An input of exactly 0 gives **0.5**.
sub: The curve is flat at both ends and steep in the middle, so the same change in the input matters most near the middle.
Very different things can be perceived as the same, such as a friend with or without a hat, just like the flat parts of the sigmoid.
Very similar things can be perceived as different, such as USC and UCLA, just like the steep middle of the sigmoid.

blocks.main: **In the code, nn.Sigmoid goes after each hidden layer.** Each hidden neuron first computes its inner product and then applies the sigmoid. The sigmoid's output is what goes to the next layer.
sub: The last layer has no sigmoid, because its outputs go to the loss, which turns them into probabilities.
Hidden sigmoid values are each between 0 and 1, but they do not have to add up to 1, so they are not a probability distribution.
blocks.end: So when a sigmoid changes a hidden value, every later layer changes too.

blocks.main: **The sigmoid comes from a discovery about real neurons.** **Lord Edgar Adrian** won the Nobel Prize in 1932 for showing that **neurons are nearly digital**, either firing or not firing. The sigmoid behaves the same way, because its output is nearly off or nearly on.
sub: Many basic ideas in AI, including neurons, inner products and near-digital firing, come from discoveries about real brains.

questions.q: Where does the idea of the sigmoid come from?
questions.a: The idea of the sigmoid comes from biology. Lord Edgar Adrian discovered that real neurons are nearly digital, either firing or not firing, and he won the Nobel Prize in 1932. The sigmoid copies this by turning any inner product into a number between 0 and 1. So a neuron is nearly off or nearly on.

questions.q: A hidden neuron's inner product is minus 2. Is its sigmoid activation closer to 0 or 1, and what does that mean?
questions.a: Its sigmoid activation is closer to 0, because the inner product is negative. So the neuron is mostly off and fires only rarely.

questions.q: If one input to that neuron goes up through a positive weight, what happens to its linear activation and its sigmoid activation?
questions.a: Both the linear activation and the sigmoid activation go up. A larger input times a positive weight raises the inner product. The sigmoid always rises when its input rises, so the neuron fires more often.

questions.q: What is the sigmoid activation if the linear activation is exactly 0?
questions.a: The sigmoid activation is 0.5, which is halfway between off and on. So the neuron is half active.

questions.q: How does the sigmoid match human perception?
questions.a: The sigmoid matches perception because some very different things are perceived as the same, and some very similar things are perceived as different. The flat parts of the sigmoid give the same output for very different inputs, such as minus 100 and minus 1000. The steep middle gives very different outputs for two nearly equal inputs on either side of zero.

blocks.main: **An LLM is built from layers, and each layer contains heads.** A **layer** is one round of improvement, and layers go one after another from the input to the output. A **head** is one expert, and it is a set of weights. Heads sit side by side inside each layer.
sub: Each head gives its own opinion on how to improve the vectors.
The layer combines all of the heads' opinions into improved vectors, and the next layer then does the same thing again.

blocks.main: **Heads and layers work like visiting a series of classes to improve yourself.** The classes you visit one after another are the **layers**. The students in each class who each give you an opinion are the **heads**.
sub: Layers give an LLM **depth**, which is one round of improvement after another.
Heads give an LLM **width**, which is many experts asked at the same time in each round.

blocks.main: **Predicting the next word is so hard that large systems have a hundred or more layers with about a hundred heads in each.** Every one of those heads learns.
sub: If the predicted next word is wrong, every head in every layer adjusts its weights with backpropagation. So the next prediction is closer to the right word.

questions.q: What are heads, and how do they relate to layers?
questions.a: A head is one expert, a set of weights that gives its own opinion on how to improve the vectors. Heads sit side by side inside each layer, and the layer combines all of their opinions into improved vectors. Layers go one after another from the input to the output, so each layer improves the vectors again.

questions.q: In the classroom of experts, what are the classes and what are the students?
questions.a: The classes are the layers, because you visit them one after another. The students in each class are the heads, because each one gives a separate opinion at the same time. You combine those opinions before moving on to the next class.

questions.q: Which gives an LLM depth and which gives it width, heads or layers?
questions.a: Layers give an LLM depth, because they are rounds of improvement that come one after another. Heads give it width, because many of them work side by side inside the same layer.

questions.q: An LLM has 5 layers with 4 heads in each layer. How many heads does it have, and which of them work at the same time?
questions.a: It has 20 heads, because each of the 5 layers has 4. The 4 heads inside one layer work side by side at the same time. The layers come one after another, so layer 2 works on the vectors that layer 1 improved.

questions.q: The LLM predicts bark instead of barks after "the dog that my parents ... ". Which weights change?
questions.a: The weights of every head in every layer change. Backpropagation assigns each weight its share of the blame for the wrong prediction. Each weight is then adjusted a little, so the next prediction is closer to barks.

questions.q: Where is the knowledge of an LLM stored?
questions.a: The knowledge of an LLM is stored in its weights. Each head is a set of weights, so the knowledge is spread across all the heads in all the layers. The vowel network's knowledge is stored in its weights in the same way.
